commits.message:
Run the throughput drill through the public ingress and at the node

e2e-stress-l2-throughput takes --route public-ingress|node. The ingress
route is a closed-loop functional check over https from one client: it keeps
at most the node's per-client in-flight cap and paces each rate class below
the node's own resolved limits. The node route is an open-loop capacity run
on the node socket with the rate limiter on, its load spread over synthetic
clients. Both refuse to run with rate limits off, and each run's config,
summary and report carry its evidence label. The nginx ingress takes its
per-address cap from the node's constant instead of its own copy.

Let the node's load generator reach the node socket as many clients

The node's per-client in-flight cap and its route-to-rate-class table are
exported from one place, so a load client can pace itself by the node's own
classes. The benchmark HTTP client moves to its own module and can reach the
node over its Unix socket, spreading its requests over synthetic client
addresses, one per /24, so a capacity run measures the node with its rate
limiter on and no per-client or per-prefix bucket binding.

Document the clean journey's settlement step

The deposit step now finishes at the L2 credit and the transfer step at
commit; the runbook and the release-readiness checks say so, and list the
cycle settlement step that observes the deposit's settlement and the
transfer's finality after the payout.

Build the routed redeemers in the traced-refusal negatives

The validation-trace negatives that rewrite an honest hop now build it with
the field item route the runner computes, so each one still reaches the
check it pins: the rewritten hop carries the stage's route, and a
substituted foreign item yield reads its item through our own field grammar
certificate. The width lifecycle harness leaves the publication-fit record
to the plain run, as the other traced publications do, since the traced run
publishes its verbose steps under the lifted envelope.

Finish settlement jobs whose event the follower has pruned (#869)

A settlement job looked up whether another operator had settled its event
through the follower's event rows, which are pruned once the event's
retirement is deeper than k. A node returning after that read "event not
found", counted failures to the cap and left the job stuck.

The event key table is never pruned, so a known key with no row now reads
as pruned. Settlement treats a pruned deposit as final, and a pruned
withdrawal as final only when its payout's conclusion is k deep or pruned
with it. The reserve-payout retry, the other job keyed to an L1 output the
follower can prune, refuses with a clear pruned error instead of building
against a gone output.

Test the ledger signature verifier startup fault through real startup

The fault test mocked our own startup modules and asserted only that
startup never got far. It now runs the real node startup with the
signature library's readiness failing (a third-party module, the only
thing replaced) and checks that startup fails at the ledger signature
verifier step with its reason after its attempts are exhausted, exiting
before the instance lock. With the verifier step removed the test fails.

Treat a lost L1 race whose effect already landed as normal, not an error

When two operators sent the same scheduler advance within a second, the
loser's transaction was refused for spent inputs, waited the 90 s recovery
window for its exact transaction, then logged ERROR and skipped the tick,
although the state it was sent for was already on chain.

submitSignedTxWithRecovery takes an optional probe for the state a
transaction is meant to reach. On a spent-inputs refusal, if that state is
already visible, or becomes visible during the unchanged recovery wait,
the outcome is lost_race: logged at info, and the caller carries on. The
wait ends early only because the intended state is seen; no bound
changed. Every other failure is unchanged. The scheduler refresh passes
"the next scheduler output appoints the operator I meant to appoint" and on
a lost race replans from it within the same tick. Merges are not wired yet.

Let the successor take its turn first at a shift end

At a shift boundary every operator holding pending work pushed the
scheduler at once, whether or not the successor already held that work, so
the successor's own takeover and the pushes raced on L1.

The tx-sharing forwarder now records, per peer operator, which pending tx
ids that peer's last catch-up answer showed it holds; inventory answers are
signed by the answering node's operator key, and an unsigned answer proves
nothing. A node that is not the successor waits the deployment's existing
new_shift_inactivity_grace_period before pushing, but only when the
successor's answer covers every pending tx; with sharing off, a failed lane,
one missing tx or any read error it pushes at once, as before. The
successor's own path and first appointment are unchanged, and no setting
was added.

Add operator commands that submit forced orders and Plutus L2 transactions

The rehearsal journey needs one forced order of each admitted shape, the
refused shapes, and normal L2 transactions including Plutus, and nothing
submitted these on Preprod.

midgard-user forced-order --shape <shape> builds and signs an L2
transaction of the named shape, screens it with the shared forced
admission check, and mints its tx-order on L1. Admitted shapes: plain,
inline-datum, native-mint, reference-input and required-signer. Refused
shapes (validity-upper-bound, plutus-mint, reference-script-output) exit 1
naming the failed check and send nothing to L1. midgard-user plutus-tx
submits an L2 transaction minting under a PlutusV3 policy and waits for
the node's verdict. Both refuse a node whose deployment marker is not the
manifest's.

The SDK's tx-order builder now needs only the hub oracle and tx-order
contracts: its hub-oracle check compares this event's policy and address,
and its validity window takes an injectable clock (Date.now by default).

Share L2 transactions between the operators of a public stack

On the public route each node sits behind a TLS ingress with no plain HTTP
port, and the attached second instance's ingress publishes on loopback
only, so the two operators could not reach each other to share L2
transactions.

When a public stack admits one producer on its own host (the attached
second instance), the harness now creates two Docker networks, one per
direction. Each ingress joins its inbound network under the certificate's
host name, each node joins the other's, and each node gets
L2_TX_PEERS=https://<host>:8443 and the stack CA through
NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS. Operator-set peers are kept. More than one producer on
the host is refused, since both ingresses serve the one host name. No node
code changes.

Give each stack fault journey the time its own budget needs

In stack mode every fault family got a fixed 2 h test limit, below its
computed journey budget at a one-hour-shift cadence, and the refusal-only
families also wait for operator-2's shift and the attestation timeouts.

The limit is now the family's computed journey budget, from the same timing
the runner reads (the stack's Shelley genesis and deployment manifest), plus
two of operator-2's shifts: one waiting for its turn and one holding the
staging. A limit no timer can hold is refused. The new test file joins the
no-devnet watcher journey list in Node CI.

Run the stack fault journeys against a public HTTPS stack

On a public stack each node sits behind a TLS ingress. The fault journeys
attached to such a stack read our node and operator-2 over HTTPS without the
stack's CA, and the operator-2 pause stopped only the node service, so the
ingress kept answering /readyz and the stop proof refused.

The stack's TLS (CA file and servername) now comes from one helper in
node-tls.ts, used by the e2e-stack controller, its process runner and the
attached journey session, which trusts it before any read. On a public stack
the pause control stops and starts the node and its ingress together; stop
proves nothing runs and /readyz is unreachable on either route, and resume
reads the ingress's own refusal (an error code, no readiness reasons) as
"not ready yet". Any other reasonless answer still fails.

Finish the clean journey's deposit and transfer steps without waiting for maturity

On a profile with a seven-day maturity the e2e-stack wallet journey waited
for three maturities in a row: the deposit step for its settlement, the
transfer step for its merge, and the withdrawal for its payout. A cycle took
about three weeks.

The deposit step now completes when the deposit credit is visible on L2, and
the transfer step at commit, after its public DA and balance checks. A new
settlement step after the withdrawal observes the deposit's settlement and
the transfer's merge (same header, confirmed ledger finalized), so every
check still runs, only later. The finalize summary reads that evidence from
the new step and refuses a settlement or merge for another event, tx or
header. Each wait keeps its existing limit and the rerun model, and the
order is the same on every profile.

Reuse only the prover's own field grammar certificate

A step now relies only on a certificate the prover controls: the builder
reuses a live Complete certificate, or resumes an InProgress one, only when
its datum owner is the prover's key, and otherwise certifies its own.

Also:
- the validation-trace workflow resolves its certificate through the
  families' shared resolver, which also checks the mint member;
- the SDK's certificate titles derive from the shared title registry;
- min-fee step 02 documents why its acceptance direction reads only the
  committed lengths;
- field-item-width-illegal step 02 gains a test that the certified route
  refuses a fixed-stride field;
- two comments in the field access and walk libraries now say what the
  code does.

Drop removed worktrees' test databases and clear week-old run folders

A worktree removed with plain `git worktree remove` left its suites'
databases on the shared test Postgres, and contrib's run folders under
the temp directory were never cleared; both piled up into the thousands.

Each `contrib test` run's cleanup now also drops databases whose checkout
hash matches no existing worktree. It uses a plain DROP, so a database
that still has a connection is skipped and reported, never forced. The
receipt records the result as `removedWorktreeCleanup`.

The first run folder a process makes now clears run folders older than a
week. Nothing reads an old run folder back.
